From 'MOO' to YOU

Many people drink milk because it is delicious and nutritious. In countries such as Australia, New Zealand and the USA, more than 95 per cent of milk comes from dairy cows. However, in some other countries, milk comes from goats, sheep, buffaloes, horses and even camels. For example, more than half of the milk produced in India comes from buffaloes.

How does cows' milk get to you? This is the journey from 'moo' to you.

1. On the dairy farm
Dairy farmers milk their cows at least twice a day. In the past, cows were milked by hand, which was very time consuming and labour intensive. Today, the milking process on modern commercial dairy farms is mostly automated. Milk is taken from dairy cows using automatic milking systems (AMS). Some systems are now controlled by robots. The milking machines pump the raw milk into refrigerated stainless steel vats, where it is stored until refrigerated tankers take it to a dairy factory. Milk must always be refrigerated so it does not deteriorate.

2. At the dairy factory
Raw milk is processed to make it safe for human consumption. The main process for treating raw milk is pasteurisation, which involves heating the milk to very high temperatures and immediately chilling it. This kills harmful bacteria and lengthens the shelf-life of the milk. After pasteurisation, milk may be made into different milk products (e.g. full cream milk, skim milk and powdered milk) and dairy products (e.g. butter, cheese, ice-cream and yoghurt), each with different packaging. The factory puts a use-by date on all packaging to let consumers, like you, know the recommended shelf-life of the product. Refrigerated trucks then transport the products to shops.

3. At the shop
The products are displayed on refrigerated shelves so you can choose what you want.

4. At home
Milk and dairy products need to be kept in the refrigerator until you consume them. You might want to check the use-by date!

questions.passage:
Read Mateo and answer questions 7 to 14.

Mateo

Mateo sat alone on the cold concrete steps beside the netball courts, waiting for his older sister to finish her shift at the canteen and drive him home. The sky was already deepening into orange, and even though he'd stopped running twenty minutes ago, his calves were still aching.

Above him, a flock of galahs bickered noisily in the branches of a huge Moreton Bay fig, their pink bellies flashing every time they shuffled along a branch. Their squabbling calls drifted down and mixed with the distant thud of a ball and the muffled shouts of swimmers still finishing laps in the pool nearby.

Mateo checked the time on the old digital watch his grandfather had given him. His sister was late, as usual. He didn't really mind. This quiet stretch after training was something he'd started to look forward to - sitting by himself, watching the last of the light fade, before the harsh security lamps clicked on and turned the courts a flat, ordinary white.

A boy he vaguely recognised from the swim squad wandered over and sat down a few steps away, dropping his bag with a thud. Mateo thought he'd seen him around before - maybe in the year below. The boy unzipped a side pocket of his bag and pulled out a small bag of lychees. They were small and rough-skinned, like little pink pebbles from a fairytale shore. He peeled one open, and the sweet, slightly floral smell drifted over immediately.

He glanced at Mateo.

'Want one?'

'Sure,' said Mateo.

The boy tossed one across, and it landed neatly in Mateo's open palm.

from Amara's Altiplano Diary

Tuesday 14 May

It felt completely unreal ... We were woken around 4 am by a soft knocking on the shutters outside our room. We scrambled into our clothes in the dark. Yolanda led us out to the llamas, where we joined her nieces (Marisol, Ines, Carla and Petra), who were already waiting astride their own animals. We stuffed our packs into the woven panniers slung across the llama's back, and I climbed onto an old stone wall, a launching point from which to swing myself up behind the saddle. It was savagely cold, even though I had on two woollen jumpers, a thermal top, Yolanda's spare poncho (a heavy striped weave I later learned had belonged to her mother) and my own waterproof shell. My legs, in nothing but thin cotton trousers, lost heat almost immediately, so Tomas wrapped a spare blanket around my knees and tucked it firmly under the saddle straps. The girls chattered and hummed to themselves the whole way. At first light, we stopped, hobbled the animals, and the girls quickly built a small fire from dry dung and twigs. It was gloriously warm. Tomas and I shared the flatbread and boiled potatoes Yolanda had packed for us.

I had assumed I'd be working alongside the girls, but it was immediately clear that wasn't the plan at all. Each of them carried a small sickle for cutting bundles of tough highland grass close to the roots. Neither Tomas nor I had been given one. I insisted on trying anyway. I grabbed a clump of grass and went to hack at it, then yelped instantly - the blades were edged like tiny saws! The girls burst out laughing. I took hold of one girl's hand to inspect it; her palms were leathery and calloused, tough as old rope.

We left the girls to their cutting and set off to climb higher, soon finding ourselves picking our way through patches of old snow. By the time we came back down, the girls had gathered enormous bundles of grass, tying them into towering loads for the llamas to carry. We made our way back towards the village on foot, the girls walking the whole way, occasionally hitching a short ride on the spare llama.

We got back around 2 pm: the girls had spent nearly ten hours gathering that day's supply of grass for winter fodder. Apparently, each season they have to walk further to find it, since the grass closest to the village has already been stripped bare.

Handwriting is an important skill

For
A letter from my granddaughter arrived this morning, and I feel compelled to write down my reaction, because it certainly wasn't the delight it should have been. The letter was clearly the product of a class assignment - each student had been asked to write to a relative - and while I was glad to hear from Maya, I found myself genuinely troubled by how poorly it was written by hand.

Parts of it were barely legible: letters were spaced unevenly, several words trailed off the line entirely, spelling mistakes littered almost every sentence, and the whole thing seemed to switch haphazardly between joined and printed letters. Why hadn't anyone checked it over before it was sent? It seems a genuine loss that handwriting, once considered a real skill worth mastering, has been allowed to slide into careless scrawl that nobody bothers to fix.

I still remember writing to cousins and pen friends as a girl, taking real pride in making each letter look tidy and presentable. These days it seems nobody minds how messy their writing is, and as a result children struggle to put a clear, readable message on paper at all. I intend to write back to Maya - in my very best handwriting - if only to show her what it should look like.

Priya

Against
Beyond the handwriting lessons scheduled at school, most students simply don't handwrite very much anymore. They don't need to, when phones, tablets and laptops handle most of their day-to-day writing. I regularly hear grown-ups complain that today's kids can no longer put a message into words - a claim I find almost funny. In reality, children today probably write more than any generation before them; it's simply not with a pen. Between texts, emails, chat messages and posts, they're constantly writing.

Spelling mistakes are certainly common in this fast, casual kind of writing, but that's a separate issue from handwriting itself - after all, someone can have beautiful handwriting and still spell terribly, or vice versa. If we're going to worry about something, spelling seems like the more useful target. Time spent drilling loops and joins in handwriting lessons might honestly be better spent teaching students to spell accurately, navigate digital tools sensibly, and type quickly and correctly.

Tech know: Microwave ovens

ACCIDENTAL DISCOVERY
In the 1940s, an American engineer named Percy Spencer was working on radar equipment when he noticed something odd: a chocolate bar in his pocket had completely melted. Curious about what had caused it, he decided to test the invisible waves from the radar equipment on other foods. When he pointed the machine at a handful of popcorn kernels, they began popping almost immediately. Percy's accidental discovery eventually led to the invention of the microwave oven, which today sits in kitchens all over the world.

HOW DOES IT WORK?
Inside every microwave oven is a device called a magnetron, which produces the invisible microwaves used for cooking. The inside walls of the oven are lined with metal, which reflects any microwaves that are not absorbed by the food straight back towards it, rather than letting them escape.

Food contains tiny molecules that behave a little like miniature magnets, with a positive end and a negative end. As microwaves pass through the food, these molecules twist rapidly back and forth to keep lining up with the changing waves. It is this constant twisting and rubbing of molecules against each other that produces heat, cooking the food from the inside as well as the outside.

Water molecules react to microwaves far more strongly than fat or sugar molecules do, which is why moist food heats up more quickly than dry food. This is also why frozen food should usually be thawed slightly, or have a small amount of water added, before microwaving - the water molecules in ice are frozen solidly in place and cannot twist and heat up as easily as liquid water can.

WHAT IS WAVELENGTH?
You may have noticed the small holes in the metal mesh covering a microwave door. Microwaves are far too wide to fit through these tiny holes, but light waves are narrow enough to pass through easily, which is how you're able to watch your food cooking. The distance between the top of one wave and the top of the very next wave is called its wavelength - and it is this measurement that decides whether or not a wave can fit through a small gap.

Genghis Khan was the founder of the Mongol Empire, which at its peak stretched across an enormous area from modern-day Korea all the way to Hungary. Before Genghis united them, twelfth-century Mongolia was home to scattered nomadic clans and farmers who frequently fought each other over access to water and grazing land. Genghis brought these rival clans together under a single banner and built one of the largest empires the world has ever seen.

Genghis was born around 1162 near the Khentii Mountains, in what is now north-central Mongolia. According to Mongol folklore, a birthmark on his hand was a sign that he was destined to become a great leader. From a young age, his mother, Hoelun, taught him about the harsh realities of tribal life and the importance of building alliances with other clans. At around nine years old, Genghis experienced this harshness firsthand when his father was poisoned by a rival clan during a shared meal. His own clan then cruelly abandoned the newly fatherless family, forcing them to fend for themselves, surviving on roots, small animals and fish. It's possible these difficult early experiences shaped the extraordinary leadership skills Genghis would later become known for.

Although Genghis is remembered for uniting the Mongol clans, he was equally feared for his ruthlessness towards anyone who resisted him. He commanded a formidable army and used military strategies still studied today, including a 'divide and conquer' approach - later used by other famous military leaders as well - which involved cutting off an enemy's lines of communication and isolating sections of their army to weaken their resolve.

Despite his fame during his lifetime, the details surrounding Genghis Khan's death and burial remain a mystery. He died in 1227, reportedly from an infected wound, but the exact location of his grave has never been found. Historians believe he may be buried somewhere near his birthplace, close to the Onon River, though many Mongolians strongly believe that searching for the site would go against his own wish to be buried without a marker.

At around nine years old, Genghis experienced this harshness firsthand when his father was poisoned by a rival clan during a shared meal. His own clan then cruelly abandoned the newly fatherless family, forcing them to fend for themselves, surviving on roots, small animals and fish. It's possible these difficult early experiences shaped the extraordinary leadership skills Genghis would later become known for.

Although Genghis is remembered for uniting the Mongol clans, he was equally feared for his ruthlessness towards anyone who resisted him. He commanded a formidable army and used military strategies still studied today, including a 'divide and conquer' approach - later used by other famous military leaders as well - which involved cutting off an enemy's lines of communication and isolating sections of their army to weaken their resolve.

Despite his fame during his lifetime, the details surrounding Genghis Khan's death and burial remain a mystery. He died in 1227, reportedly from an infected wound, but the exact location of his grave has never been found. Historians believe he may be buried somewhere near his birthplace, close to the Onon River, though many Mongolians strongly believe that searching for the site would go against his own wish to be buried without a marker.

The billabong welcomes us like an old friend,
murmurs low along its muddy rim
and cools our ankles with a lazy swirl.

Dragonflies holiday here too, hovering

Gum trees lean in close, peeling
their papery bark in long curling strips,
their pale reflections wavering below.

At dusk the sky splits into orange fire,
threads of woodsmoke rising
to tangle with the last light of day.

At dawn the air fills with insect static,
the abrupt clatter of a startled cockatoo,
white flashes scattered through green.

Our days blur softly into one another;
the billabong stays exactly as it is -
it never has to pack the car and leave.
